Part 3: Does Reflow Straighten the Paths?¶

Hypothesis: One round of reflow will make the sampling paths straighter, so with very few steps (1–5) the dots will land closer to the B than the baseline, while quality at many steps stays about the same.

Made 50000 pairs in 3.7 s

Reflow extra cost: making pairs 3.7 s + training 5.6 s = 9.3 s
Compute-matched baseline extra training: 5.7 s

Task 3. With the same weights and starting noise, 1 step gives a blob: every dot moves once using the velocity at t = 0, which is only an average direction. Quality improves quickly up to about 25 steps, then levels off around 0.15, while the best possible score (two real B samples) is about 0.09. Sampling time grows in proportion to the number of steps, since each step is one network call. The gap that remains after leveling off is not caused by too few steps. It comes from the learned model (blurry edges, points between strokes) and the target representation (pixel grid, 40×40 histogram), and more steps can't fix an inaccurate model.

Part 3, Task 3: What the evidence supports¶

Result. The evidence supports the hypothesis for few-step sampling. Over 3 seeds, reflow reached a histogram difference of 0.179 ± 0.004 with a single Euler step, versus 0.978 ± 0.008 for the baseline. Reflow reached its best quality by about 5 steps, while the baseline needed about 25 steps to match it. Because every network call costs about the same, this means roughly 25x fewer network calls for similar quality. Path straightness (extra distance travelled compared with a straight line) dropped from 0.51 to about 0.0001.

Alternative explanation: extra training. The reflow model got 6,000 more training steps than the baseline. To rule this out, I trained a compute-matched baseline for the same 6,000 extra steps on the original random pairs. It did not improve (0.977 at 1 step, straightness 0.51), so the gain comes from the paired data, not extra training.

Straighter is not the same as more accurate. At 25 steps, all three models score about 0.163–0.167, with differences inside seed noise. Reflow did not make the final shape better; it made the same shape reachable in fewer steps. All models stay well above the best possible score (about 0.091, two independent samples of the true B), so the remaining error comes from the learned model, not from the number of steps.

Inherited errors. Reflow learns from the baseline's generated endpoints, not from the true B. Any mistakes the baseline makes (blurry edges, points between the letter's strokes) are copied into the reflow training data, so reflow cannot be more accurate than the baseline it learned from.

Cost. Reflow needed 9.3 s of one-time extra work (3.7 s to generate 50,000 pairs + 5.6 s training). This is paid once, while the savings apply to every later sample.

Limits. Only 3 seeds, one target shape (the letter B), one round of reflow, and one quality metric (a 40x40 histogram, which can miss fine details). The held-out test noise was never used to build the reflow pairs.

Setup and reproducibility¶

Item Value
Model MLP: input (x, y, t) → 128 → 128 → 128 → 2, SiLU activations, 33,794 parameters
Training Adam, learning rate 1e-3, batch 256, 30,000 steps (31-40 s)
Target Letter "B" drawn with matplotlib (bold font) on a 200×200 image; points = random letter pixels + uniform jitter, scaled so the letter spans −2 to 2 vertically
Reflow 50,000 pairs made with 100 Euler steps (3.7 s); reflow model = copy of baseline + 6,000 steps on pairs (5.6 s)
Compute-matched baseline copy of baseline + 6,000 steps on original random pairs (5.7 s)
Quality metric 40×40 histogram on [−3, 3]², plus one extra bin for points outside; score = half the summed absolute difference
Seeds training 0 (plus 1 and 2 for the seed check), animation noise 1, step comparison 123, reflow pairs 2026, held-out test 999
